title: 2 Chronicles 30:13–27
context: A great assembly gathers in the second month, removes the altars in Jerusalem, and keeps the Passover and the feast of unleavened bread. Many from the northern tribes had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover other than the way it is written, and Hezekiah prayed that the good LORD would pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God, even if they were not clean by the purification of the sanctuary; the LORD listened to Hezekiah and healed the people. The festival is extended for another seven days with generous offerings from the king and princes, and the joy is described as unmatched in Jerusalem since the time of Solomon. The Levitical priests bless the people, and their prayer comes up to God’s holy habitation in heaven. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage, including 30:18–20, as shared ground about God’s mercy toward those who seek him with the heart and the joy of renewed worship (compare 1 Samuel 16:7).

verses.text: Many people assembled at Jerusalem to keep the feast of unleavened bread in the second month, a very great assembly.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see many people gathering in Jerusalem to keep the feast of unleavened bread. The response to the invitation is very great.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assembly as God’s blessing on the call to return. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a joyful sign of renewal.

verses.text: They arose and took away the altars that were in Jerusalem, and they took away all the altars for incense and threw them into the brook Kidron.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people removing the altars and incense altars in Jerusalem and throwing them into the brook Kidron. Repentance includes removing idols.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cleansing of false worship as a necessary part of returning to the LORD. Both traditions commonly read the verse as zeal for pure worship.

verses.text: Then they killed the Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month. The priests and the Levites were ashamed, and sanctified themselves, and brought burnt offerings into the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Passover kept on the fourteenth day of the second month, and the ashamed priests and Levites sanctifying themselves. The people’s zeal stirs the leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the priests’ shame leading to renewed consecration. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sign that renewal can spread from the people to their leaders.

verses.text: They stood in their place after their order, according to the law of Moses the man of God. The priests sprinkled the blood which they received of the hand of the Levites.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests and Levites standing in their places according to the law of Moses. Order and obedience mark the worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the careful observance as worship shaped by God’s word. Both traditions commonly read the verse as balancing joy with faithful order.

verses.text: For there were many in the assembly who had not sanctified themselves; therefore the Levites were in charge of killing the Passovers for everyone who was not clean, to sanctify them to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that many had not sanctified themselves, so the Levites killed the Passover lambs on their behalf. Care is taken so that the unprepared can still take part.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Levites’ service as gracious provision for the weak. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing pastoral concern within the worship.

verses.text: For a multitude of the people, even many of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover other than the way it is written. For Hezekiah had prayed for them, saying, “May the good LORD pardon everyone
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see many from the north eating the Passover other than as written, and Hezekiah praying for the good LORD to pardon them. Mercy meets imperfect but sincere seekers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s intercession as appealing to God’s goodness rather than to ritual completeness. Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s mercy toward those who seek him.

verses.text: who sets his heart to seek God, the LORD, the God of his fathers, even if they aren’t clean according to the purification of the sanctuary.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the prayer for everyone who sets his heart to seek God, even if not ritually clean. The heart’s seeking matters most to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prayer as recognizing that God looks on the heart (compare 1 Samuel 16:7; Psalm 51:17). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as valuing sincere seeking without dismissing God’s ordinances.

verses.text: The LORD listened to Hezekiah, and healed the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD listening to Hezekiah and healing the people. God responds to intercession with healing mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the healing as God’s gracious answer to prayer offered for his people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God hearing prayer and restoring those who seek him.

verses.text: The children of Israel who were present at Jerusalem kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with great gladness. The Levites and the priests praised the LORD day by day, singing with loud instruments to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people keeping the feast seven days with great gladness while the Levites and priests praise the LORD. Joy fills the renewed worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gladness as the fruit of restored fellowship with God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of wholehearted, joyful worship.

verses.text: Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who had good understanding in the service of the LORD. So they ate throughout the feast for the seven days, offering sacrifices of peace offerings and making confession to the LORD, the God of their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah encouraging the Levites who had good understanding, and the people offering peace offerings and confession. Leadership supports faithful service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see confession and peace offerings together as reflecting both humility and fellowship with God. Both traditions commonly read the verse as honoring skilled service and sincere worship.

verses.text: The whole assembly took counsel to keep another seven days, and they kept another seven days with gladness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the assembly choosing to keep another seven days with gladness. Joy overflows beyond the appointed time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the extension as a sign of hearts stirred by God’s grace. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a spontaneous expression of thankfulness.

verses.text: For Hezekiah king of Judah gave to the assembly for offerings one thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep; and the princes gave to the assembly a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep; and a great number of priests sanctified themselves.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah and the princes providing many bulls and sheep, and many priests sanctifying themselves. Generosity and consecration go together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the leaders’ generosity as setting an example for the people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that worship involves costly giving.

verses.text: All the assembly of Judah, with the priests and the Levites, and all the assembly who came out of Israel, and the foreigners who came out of the land of Israel and who lived in Judah, rejoiced.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Judah, the priests and Levites, those from Israel, and the foreigners living in Judah rejoicing together. The celebration is inclusive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusion of foreigners as a hint of God’s wider purposes. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of unity among God’s people.

verses.text: So there was great joy in Jerusalem; for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there was nothing like this in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see great joy in Jerusalem, unmatched since Solomon’s time. The renewal is remembered as truly historic.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comparison with Solomon as linking Hezekiah’s reform with the glory of the temple’s dedication (compare 1 Kings 8:66). Both traditions commonly read the verse as celebrating God’s restoring grace.

verses.text: Then the Levitical priests arose and blessed the people. Their voice was heard, and their prayer came up to his holy habitation, even to heaven.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levitical priests blessing the people and their prayer reaching God’s holy habitation in heaven. God hears the prayers of his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the blessing as God’s favor resting on his people through appointed means. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a fitting close to a season of renewal.
